paras: The lynching of Jeff was the hanging of a Black man in Louisiana in late June 1881, after he was accused of attacking the daughter of W. R. Turnage, his employer. The Farmerville Gazette's account, reprinted in three Louisiana papers, defended the killing as a case that did not admit of "law's delay."

Jeff had been jailed on a charge of raping an old Black woman, but because she was said to be "crazy" the state could not try him; released on a nominal bond that Turnage signed, he went to work on Turnage's farm.

According to the Gazette, while the parents were away, the eldest daughter found Jeff under the house with a knife and club; he followed her, and after a scuffle she shut herself inside. When he struck the door with an axe, she shot him through it with a revolver, in the thigh by the Gazette's account and the hip by the Donaldsonville Chief's.

Jeff fled, and that evening Turnage, his son and some neighbors lay in wait in the D'Outre swamp and near the stock lot. He was captured near the cow-pen about dark and the next morning was seen hanging from a tree at the swamp's edge, where the body remained over twenty-four hours.
The accounts do not say who hanged him, and no report of an inquest, arrest or official response appears in the coverage.

Every account comes from one local white source: the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe printed the Gazette's June 29 story in full on July 8 under "NEGRO LYNCHED," and the Richland Beacon of Rayville reprinted it on July 16. The Gazette told the story from the Turnage family's side, calling Jeff "an enraged and brutal negro," remarking that the body might "be there yet for ought we know," and closing that such cases "do not admit of law's delay, especially in an attempted outrage upon a daughter or sister." The Donaldsonville Chief ran a shorter version credited to the "Union Gazette" on July 9, without the closing comment, though it called Jeff "the scoundrel."

reader.title: Lynching of Jeff (Louisiana, 1881)
bases: A Black man accused of attacking a farmer's daughter was captured by the farmer and his neighbors and found hanging from a tree the next morning (A2, A3).

Jeff was found hanging from a tree after his capture by Turnage, his son and 'some neighbors', with no officer or legal process reported (A2, A3); the Gazette justified it as a case that did 'not admit of law's delay' after an alleged 'attempted outrage' (A2). Who did the hanging is not named, so the group size rests on the capturing party.
All three printings derive from one local white paper, the Farmerville Gazette of June 29 (A2, A4) or the 'Union Gazette' (A3), and no independent account was found.

accounts.label: Farmerville Gazette (local white paper)
accounts.gist: Jeff, found under the house armed with a knife and club, chased Miss Turnage, struck the door with an axe, was shot in the thigh, and was captured near the cow-pen at dark by men lying in wait; next morning he hung from a tree at the swamp's edge.

accounts.label: Union Gazette, as condensed by the Donaldsonville Chief
accounts.gist: Jeff 'assaulted' the daughter, was shot in the hip while breaking the door, hid in the woods, and was pursued and captured by Turnage and his neighbors; his body was found hanging the next morning.

framing.detail: The Gazette text, run under 'NEGRO LYNCHED', called Jeff 'an enraged and brutal negro', praised Miss Turnage as 'equal to the emergency', and closed that such cases 'do not admit of law's delay'.
The Donaldsonville Chief ran a shortened version among parish news without the closing comment, though it called Jeff 'the scoundrel'.

conflicts.note: Minor; the fuller Gazette text says thigh.

record_check.dossier: The attack and capture were on 'last Wednesday' before the Gazette of June 29, probably June 22; the body was seen hanging the next morning, probably June 23. No paper prints the date.
